p.bold: Truly Functional Solutions to the Longest Uptrend Problem

body.p: ALEXANDER DINGES , RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau, Germany RALF HINZE , RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau, Germany

Solutions to the longest increasing subsequence problem are typically implemented imperatively, relyingon arrays for constant-time lookups and updates. Replacing these arrays with functional sequences allowsa purely functional solution with the same asymptotic running time, but with significantly worse practicalperformance. In this pearl, we present a purely functional approach that is not only asymptotically optimal,but also efficient in practice. The core idea is to exploit the interplay between search, lookup, and updateoperations through Huet’s zipper. In addition, we improve the adaptive behaviour of imperative solutionscommonly found in the literature.
CCS Concepts: • Theory of computation → Data structures design and analysis ; • Software and its engineering → Functional languages .
Additional Key Words and Phrases: Longest Increasing Subsequence, Zipper, Haskell

Alexander Dinges and Ralf Hinze. 2025. Truly Functional Solutions to the Longest Uptrend Problem (FunctionalPearl). ACM Reference Format: Proc. ACM Program. Lang. 9, ICFP, Article 251 (August 2025), 16 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3747520

sec.title: 1 Introduction
sec.p: Oscar Wilde, Lady Windermere’s Fan I can resist anything except temptation.

“Shall I be pure or impure?” Many temptations lure the functional programmer: input/output,exceptions, references, and, in particular, arrays with constant-time update. And the sirens whisper:“Haskell is the world’s finest imperative programming language.” We openly admit that we toohave succumbed to temptation: on more than one occasion, the efficiency promises of updatablearrays have been too compelling. Here is a recent example.We derived an algorithm for solving the “longest increasing subsequence” problem. Briefly, givena sequence of elements, the problem is to find a longest subsequence that is strictly increasing. Asubsequence is given by a selection of the original data, such that the relative order of the data itemsis preserved. The derived algorithm can justifiably be called imperative, and indeed we used thefacts, using pseudo-code rather than monadic code to emphasize its imperative nature. If each operation — search, look-up, and update — runs in logarithmic time, then the asymptoticrunning time is no worse than that of the imperative fragment. However, the constant factors areworse, as look-up and update do not run in constant-time; and, indeed, benchmarks demonstratethe superiority of the imperative program.We gave up ... but the problem gnawed at us. After a while, we realized that we had beenguilty of imperative thinking. The three operations — search, look-up, and update — are closelyintertwined, but they communicate rather indirectly via numerical positions, via indices. Surelythere is a better way of arranging their interplay. This pearl tells the story of a truly functionalsolution to the “longest increasing subsequence” problem (“longest uptrend” for short). sec.title: 5 Conclusion
sec.p: All in all, this was an enjoyable exercise in algorithm, data structure, and interface design. Our firstattempts at purely functional solutions to the “longest uptrend” problem focused on implementing searchable , indexable sequence types, supporting the following interface.
::::::(!):: Sequ Type → Type nil Sequ a cons a → Sequ a → Sequ a Sequ a → Int → a update :: Sequ a → Int → a → Sequ a search :: ( a → Bool ) → Sequ a → Int

We tried out several data structures, but the efforts did not pay off. Simply replacing ephemeralarrays with these persistent sequence types worsened the running time by an order of magnitude.Abstracting slightly from the details of our application (renamingto Spine to Sequ and a ⇒ Spine a Pos a ), our finger trees can be used to implement a radically different interface.
:::::::: Sequ Type → Type nil Sequ a cons a → Sequ a → Sequ a search :: ( a → Bool ) → Sequ a →( Maybe ( Pos a , a ) , Maybe ( Pos a , a )) Pos Type → Type apply :: Pos a → a → Sequ a

The revised interface is much more restrictive, but at the same time also much safer. The indices,the numerical positions, have disappeared from the scene — no “index out of range” errors anymore.Indices are replaced by paths. The functionbe “applied” to a value to update the original sequence, replacing the general update mechanismbased on numerical positions. This interface works beautifully for the “longest uptrend” problem.Whether it has other uses remains to be seen.We have also gained some algorithmic insights. An important part of the lazy functional DNAis the idea of turning control structures into data structures: binary trees are the manifestationof binary search. Maybe this is old news to you, but it was new to us that finger trees are theincarnation of exponential search.In conclusion, it is pleasing to see that we can keep up with or even surpass the imperativeprogram. But, what was the crucial step in achieving this goal? We say the introduction of Huet’szipper! This enabled us to organize the interplay of search, look-up, and update much more neatly.So, three cheers to Gérard! search returns two positions; each of these positions can

To evaluate the performance of our zipper-based implementations, we benchmark them against afew alternatives. In total, we compare six different implementations.
• ST-Arrays: The imperative solution, see Figuresublanguage, using thefor comparison. 1 , transliterated into Haskell’s imperative ST -monad and ST -arrays. This implementation serves as the baseline
• ST-Arrays-Exponential-Search: An adaptation of the imperative solution, that uses expo-nential search instead of binary search to determine the tipping point.

• Random-Access-Lists: A functional variant of the imperative solution, using persistentsequences based on node-oriented random-access lists. Look-up, update, and search aresupported in logarithmic time, so the implementation is asymptotically optimal.

• ADwH: An implementation taken from the textbookwhich is developed in a series of exercises (11.6–11.8). The solution is based on AVL-trees.Interestingly, it also avoids indices: In the update step, the AVL-tree is split at the tippingpoint and then merged with the new element replacing the old.
